e-564.knowledge_point: Finding the Time Intervals on which a Particle is Moving in a Particular Direction
e-564.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\textrm m / \textrm s^2,$ given by the function $a(t) = 3t^2+2t-6,$ where $t > 0$ is the time in seconds. The positive direction is left to right. If the particle is stationary when $t=0\,\textrm s,$ determine the time intervals in which the particle is moving to the right.
e-564.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (3{t}^{2}+2t-6)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{3}+{t}^{2}-6t+C\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the particle is stationary at the time $t=0.$ This means $v(0) = 0,$ so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =(0)^{3}+(0)^{2}-6(0)+C \\ 0 & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore the velocity of the particle is

$$
v(t) = t^3+t^2-6t.
$$

To find the time interval in which the particle is moving to the *right*, we must solve the inequality $v > 0.$ This gives

$$
t^3+t^2-6t = t(t+3)(t-2) > 0.
$$

Plotting the graph of $v(t),$ we get the following picture.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14094087/assets/03b5ff6282d59038cbb355c0c3f017b544f286228ba4c3a82329897b4b43674c.png)

The particle moves to the right when $v(t)$ is positive. So, from the graph, we see that the particle moves to the right when $t>2.$

e-565.knowledge_point: Finding the Times at Which a Particle Reaches Its Maximum Velocity
e-565.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\textrm m / \textrm s^2,$ given by the function $a(t) = 6t-3t^2,$ where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=2\,\textrm m / \textrm s$ when $t=1\,\textrm s,$ calculate the maximum velocity $v_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
e-565.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\dfrac{\textrm d v}{\textrm d t} = a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t) = 0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t) = 0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 6t-3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ 3t(2-t) & =0 \\ t & =0,\,2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t> 0$, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t = 2\,\textrm s.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{″}(t) & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6t-3{t}^{2}) \\  & =6-6t \\ {v}^{″}(2) & =6-6(2) \\  & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

Since $v''(2) <      0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=2\,\textrm s.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (6t-3{t}^{2})\text{d}t \\  & =3{t}^{2}-{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1) = 2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3(1)^{2}-(1)^{3}+C & =2 \\ 3-1+C & =2\,⟹\,C=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t) =3t^2-t^3.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
v_{\text{max}}= v(2) = 3(2)^2 - (2)^3 =4\,\textrm m / \textrm s
$$

So the maximum velocity $v_{\text{max}}=4\,\textrm m / \textrm s$ is reached at $t=2\,\textrm s.$

e-7226.knowledge_point: Finding the Times at Which a Particle is Stationary
e-7226.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\textrm m / \textrm s^2,$ given by the function $a(t) =2t-6$, where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=4\,\textrm m / \textrm s$ when $t=1\,\textrm s$, determine the moments in time when the particle is stationary.
e-7226.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\textrm m / \textrm s.$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2t-6)\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{2}-6t+C.\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1) =4.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =(1)^{2}-6(1)+C \\ 4 & =-5+C \\ C & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t) = t^2-6t + 9.$

Now, we find the moments in time when $v=0\,\textrm m / \textrm s\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-6t+9 & =0 \\ (t-3)^{2} & =0 \\ t & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particle is stationary when $t=3 \,\textrm s.$

content.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=2t-4,$ where $t>0$ is the time in seconds.  The positive direction is left to right. If the particle has velocity $v=12\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=6\,\text{s},$ determine the time intervals in which the particle moves to the left.
content.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2t-4)\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{2}-4t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(6)=12.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}12 & =(6)^{2}-4(6)+C \\ 12 & =12+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)={t}^{2}-4t.$

To find the time interval in which the particle is moving to the *left*, we must solve the inequality $v<0.$ This gives

$$
{t}^{2}-4t=t(t-4)<0.
$$

Plotting the graph of $v(t)$, we get the following picture.

before.html:
Question 4
?

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, given by the function a(t)=1−2t, where t>0 is the time in seconds. The positive direction is left to right. If the particle has velocity v=−6m/s when t=4s, determine the time intervals in which the particle moves to the right.

a
 t>6
b
 0<t<3
c
 2<t<4
d
 t>3
e
 3<t<6
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating gives v(t)=t-t^2+C. Using v(4)=-6 yields C=6, so v(t)=-(t-3)(t+2). For t>0, velocity is positive exactly when 0<t<3, so the particle moves right on that interval.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=1-2t$, where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. The positive direction is left to right. If the particle has velocity $v=-6\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=4\,\text{s}$, determine the time intervals in which the particle moves to the right.
after.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (1-2t)\text{d}t \\  & =t-{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(4)=-6.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-6 & =(4)-(4)^{2}+C \\ -6 & =4-16+C \\ -6 & =-12+C \\ C & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=-{t}^{2}+t+6.$

To find the time interval in which the particle is moving to the *right*, we must solve the inequality $v>0.$ This gives

$$
-{t}^{2}+t+6=-({t}^{2}-t-6)=-(t+2)(t-3)>0.
$$

Plotting the graph of $v(t),$ we get the following picture.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14094087/assets/74db16dc00f5d08637cef02960409b7fd15c4bd3c19f577fa5a1f30ac8c402d3.png)

From the graph, we see that $v>0$ whenever $0<t<3.$

Question 5
?

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, a(t)=2t−5, where t>0 is the time in seconds. The positive direction is left to right. If the particle has velocity v=10m/s when t=6s, determine the time intervals in which the particle moves to the left.

a
0<t<1
b
0<t<4
c
t>4
d
1<t<4
e
 t>1
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating gives v(t)=t^2-5t+C. Since v(6)=10, 10=36-30+C, so C=4. Thus v(t)=(t-1)(t-4), which is negative exactly when 1<t<4. Negative velocity means moving left.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ $a(t)=2t-5,$ where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. The positive direction is left to right. If the particle has velocity $v=10\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=6\,\text{s},$ determine the time intervals in which the particle moves to the left.
after.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2t-5)\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{2}-5t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(6)=10.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}10 & =(6)^{2}-5(6)+C \\ 10 & =6+C \\ C & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)={t}^{2}-5t+4.$

To find the time interval in which the particle is moving to the *left*, we must solve the inequality $v<0.$ This gives

$$
{t}^{2}-5t+4=(t-1)(t-4)<0.
$$

Plotting the graph of $v(t)$, we get the following picture.

Question 5

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, a(t)=2t−5, where t>0 is the time in seconds. The positive direction is left to right. If the particle has velocity v=10m/s when t=6s, determine the time intervals in which the particle moves to the left.

a
0<t<1
b
0<t<4
c
t>4
d
1<t<4
e
 t>1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find v(t) by integrating the acceleration with respect to time: v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫(2t−5)dt=t2−5t+C

To determine C, we use the fact that v(6)=10. Substituting this into the above gives 10=(6)2−5(6)+C10=6+CC=4.

Therefore, the velocity v of the particle at time t is v(t)=t2−5t+4.

To find the time interval in which the particle is moving to the left, we must solve the inequality v<0. This gives

t2−5t+4=(t−1)(t−4)<0.

Plotting the graph of v(t), we get the following picture.

From the graph, we see that v<0 whenever 1<t<4.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Time Intervals on which a Particle is Moving in a Particular Direction
content.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ $a(t)=2t-5,$ where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. The positive direction is left to right. If the particle has velocity $v=10\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=6\,\text{s},$ determine the time intervals in which the particle moves to the left.
content.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2t-5)\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{2}-5t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(6)=10.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}10 & =(6)^{2}-5(6)+C \\ 10 & =6+C \\ C & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)={t}^{2}-5t+4.$

To find the time interval in which the particle is moving to the *left*, we must solve the inequality $v<0.$ This gives

$$
{t}^{2}-5t+4=(t-1)(t-4)<0.
$$

Plotting the graph of $v(t)$, we get the following picture.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14094087/assets/ad76f817f7c6e4a254e8881c34270eb875e72d821531566cb141cb393dcead72.png)

From the graph, we see that $v<0$ whenever $1<t<4.$

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=5-\frac{1}{2}t,$ where $t⩾0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=3\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=4\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.

The maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}=$
{{field-1}}
$\text{m}/\text{s}$ is reached at $t=$
{{field-2}}$\text{s}.$
after.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 5-\frac{1}{2}t & =0 \\ t & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t=10\,\text{s}.$

We now test the extreme values using the second derivative test. The second derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5-\frac{1}{2}t) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(10)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=10\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (5-\frac{1}{2}t)\text{d}t \\  & =5t-\frac{1}{4}{t}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(4)=3.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}5(4)-\frac{1}{4}(4)^{2}+C & =3 \\ 20-4+C & =3\,⟹\,C=-13.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity is given by $v(t)=5t-\frac{1}{4}{t}^{2}-13.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(10)=5(10)-\frac{1}{4}(10)^{2}-13=12\,\text{m}/\text{s}.
$$

So the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}=12\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ is reached at $t=10\,\text{s}.$

before.html:
Question 7
?

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, given by the function a(t)=4−t2, where t>0 is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity v=0m/s when t=0s, calculate the maximum velocity vmax of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.

a
vmax=143m/s,t=2s
b
vmax=113m/s,t=1s
c
vmax=163m/s,t=2s
d
vmax=13m/s,t=1s
e
vmax=83m/s,t=2s
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating and using v(0)=0 gives v(t)=4t-t^3/3. Acceleration is positive for 0<t<2 and negative for t>2, so velocity reaches its global maximum at t=2. Then v(2)=8-8/3=16/3 m/s.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=4-{t}^{2}$, where $t>0$ is the time  in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
after.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 4-{t}^{2} & =0 \\ (2-t)(2+t) & =0 \\ t & =\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t⩾0$, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t=2\,\text{s}.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{″}(t) & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4-{t}^{2}) \\  & =-2t \\ {v}^{″}(2) & =-2(2) \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(2)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=2\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (4-{t}^{2})\text{d}t \\  & =4t-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4(0)-\frac{1}{3}(0)^{3}+C & =0 \\ 0+0+C & =0\,⟹\,C=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=4t-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(2)=4(2)-\frac{1}{3}(2)^{3}=\frac{16}{3}\,\text{m}/\text{s}
$$

EXPLANATION

a(t)=04−t2=0(2−t)(2+t)=0t=±2.

Since t⩾0, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when t=2s.

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of v(t) and evaluate it at t=2:

v″(t)=d2vdt2=ddt(dvdt)=ddt(a(t))=ddt(4−t2)=−2tv″(2)=−2(2)=−4.

Since v″(2)<0, we conclude that the velocity is maximized when t=2s.

Now, we find v(t) by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫(4−t2)dt=4t−13t3+C To determine C, we use the fact that v(0)=0. Substituting this into the above gives 4(0)−13(0)3+C=00+0+C=0⟹C=0. Therefore, the velocity v of the particle at time t is v(t)=4t−13t3.

vmax=v(2)=4(2)−13(2)3=163m/s

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Times at Which a Particle Reaches Its Maximum Velocity
content.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=4-{t}^{2}$, where $t>0$ is the time  in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
content.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 4-{t}^{2} & =0 \\ (2-t)(2+t) & =0 \\ t & =\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t⩾0$, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t=2\,\text{s}.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{″}(t) & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4-{t}^{2}) \\  & =-2t \\ {v}^{″}(2) & =-2(2) \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(2)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=2\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (4-{t}^{2})\text{d}t \\  & =4t-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4(0)-\frac{1}{3}(0)^{3}+C & =0 \\ 0+0+C & =0\,⟹\,C=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=4t-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(2)=4(2)-\frac{1}{3}(2)^{3}=\frac{16}{3}\,\text{m}/\text{s}
$$

decision.explanation: Integrating gives v(t)=3t-t^3+C. Using v(2)=2 yields C=4. Acceleration is positive for 0≤t<1 and negative for t>1, so velocity reaches its global maximum at t=1. Then v(1)=3-1+4=6 m/s.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=3-3{t}^{2},$ where $t⩾0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=2\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=2\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time whan the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
after.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 3-3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ 3(1-t)(1+t) & =0 \\ t & =\pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t⩾0$, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t=1\,\text{s}.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{″}(t) & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3-3{t}^{2}) \\  & =-6t \\ {v}^{″}(1) & =-6(1) \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(1)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=1\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (3-3{t}^{2})\text{d}t \\  & =3t-{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(2)=2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3(2)-{2}^{3}+C & =2 \\ 6-8+C & =2\,⟹\,C=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=4+3t-{t}^{3}.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(1)=4+3(1)-{1}^{3}=6\,\text{m}/\text{s}
$$

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=7-7{t}^{2},$ where $t⩾0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=1\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=2\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity. Do not round your answer.

The maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}=$
{{field-1}}
$\text{m}/\text{s}$ is reached at $t=$
{{field-2}}$\text{s}.$
after.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 7-7{t}^{2} & =0 \\ 7(1-t)(1+t) & =0 \\ t & =\pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t⩾0$, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t=1\,\text{s}.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{″}(t) & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(7-7{t}^{2}) \\  & =-14t \\ {v}^{″}(1) & =-14(1) \\  & =-14.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(1)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=1\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (7-7{t}^{2})\text{d}t \\  & =7t-\frac{7}{3}{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(2)=1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}7(2)-\frac{7}{3}(2)^{3}+C & =1 \\ 14-\frac{56}{3}+C & =1\,⟹\,C=\frac{17}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{17}{3}+7t-\frac{7}{3}{t}^{3}.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(1)=\frac{17}{3}+7(1)-\frac{7}{3}(1)^{3}=\frac{31}{3}\,\text{m}/\text{s}
$$

So the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}=\frac{31}{3}\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ is reached at $t=1\,\text{s}.$

If the particle has velocity v=14m/s when t=1s, calculate the maximum velocity vmax of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.

vmax=37.5m/s,t=5s

vmax=38m/s,t=5s

decision.explanation: Integrating gives v(t)=15t-(3/2)t^2+C. Using v(1)=14 gives C=1/2. Acceleration changes from positive to negative at t=5, so velocity reaches its global maximum there: v(5)=75-37.5+0.5=38 m/s.

\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(15-3t) \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(5)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=5\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (15-3t)\text{d}t \\  & =15t-\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(1)=14.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}15(1)-\frac{3}{2}(1)^{2}+C & =14 \\ C & =\frac{3}{2}-1\,⟹\,C=\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{1}{2}+15t-\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(5)=\frac{1}{2}+15(5)-\frac{3}{2}(5)^{2}=38\,\text{m}/\text{s}
$$

Question 10

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, given by the function a(t)=15−3t, where t>0 is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity v=14m/s when t=1s, calculate the maximum velocity vmax of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.

a
vmax=37.5m/s,t=5s
b
vmax=38m/s,t=5s
c
vmax=24.5m/s,t=2s
d
vmax=14m/s,t=1s
e
vmax=75m/s,t=5s
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The extrema of the velocity v occur at the critical points of v.

Since dvdt=a(t), to find the times where v is a maximum, we just need to solve a(t)=0 and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving a(t)=0 gives

a(t)=015−3t=0t=5.

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when t=5s.

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of v(t): d2vdt2=ddt(dvdt)=ddt(a(t))=ddt(15−3t)=−3

Since v″(5)<0, we conclude that the velocity is maximized when t=5s.

Now, we find v(t) by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫(15−3t)dt=15t−32t2+C

To determine C, we use the fact that v(1)=14. Substituting this into the above gives 15(1)−32(1)2+C=14C=32−1⟹C=12. Therefore, the velocity v of the particle at time t is v(t)=12+15t−32t2.

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

vmax=v(5)=12+15(5)−32(5)2=38m/s

content.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=15-3t,$ where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=14\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=1\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
content.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 15-3t & =0 \\ t & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t=5\,\text{s}.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(15-3t) \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(5)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=5\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (15-3t)\text{d}t \\  & =15t-\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(1)=14.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}15(1)-\frac{3}{2}(1)^{2}+C & =14 \\ C & =\frac{3}{2}-1\,⟹\,C=\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{1}{2}+15t-\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(5)=\frac{1}{2}+15(5)-\frac{3}{2}(5)^{2}=38\,\text{m}/\text{s}
$$

before.html:
Question 11
?

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, given by the function a(t)=(2t+1)3, where t>0 is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity v=658m/s when t=1s, determine the moment in time when the particle is stationary.

a
t=12s
b
t=3s
c
t=32s
d
t=1s
e
t=2s
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating gives v(t)=(2t+1)^4/8+C. Since v(1)=65/8, C=-2. Setting v(t)=0 gives (2t+1)^4=16. For t>0, 2t+1 is positive, so 2t+1=2 and t=1/2 s.

after.name: Question 11
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=(2t+1)^{3}$, where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=\frac{65}{8}\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=1\,\text{s}$, determine the moment in time when the particle is stationary.
after.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2t+1)^{3}\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{8}(2t+1)^{4}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1)=\frac{65}{8}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{65}{8} & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot {[2(1)+1]}^{4}+C \\ \frac{65}{8} & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot (81)+C \\ C & =\frac{65}{8}-\frac{81}{8} \\ C & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{1}{8}(2t+1)^{4}-2.$

Now, we find the moments in time when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{8}(2t+1)^{4}-2 & =0 \\ (2t+1)^{4} & =16 \\ 2t+1 & =\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions are $t=-\frac{3}{2}\,,\frac{1}{2}.$

Since $t>0$, we discard solution $t=-\frac{3}{2}.$ 
Therefore, the particle is stationary when $t=\frac{1}{2}\,\text{s}.$

Question 11

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, given by the function a(t)=(2t+1)3, where t>0 is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity v=658m/s when t=1s, determine the moment in time when the particle is stationary.

a
t=12s
b
t=3s
c
t=32s
d
t=1s
e
t=2s
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The particle is stationary when v=0m/s.

First, we find v(t) by integrating the acceleration with respect to time: v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫(2t+1)3dt=18(2t+1)4+C To determine C, we use the fact that v(1)=658. Substituting this into the above gives 658=18⋅[2(1)+1]4+C658=18⋅(81)+CC=658−818C=−2. Therefore, the velocity v of the particle at time t is v(t)=18(2t+1)4−2.

Now, we find the moments in time when v=0m/s:

18(2t+1)4−2=0(2t+1)4=162t+1=±2.

The solutions are t=−32,12.

Since t>0, we discard solution t=−32. Therefore, the particle is stationary when t=12s.

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, given by the function a(t)=t−t3/2, where t>0 is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity v=415m/s when t=1s, determine the moment in time when the particle is stationary.

a
t=35s
b
t=115s
c
t=13s
d
t=53s
e
t=310s
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating gives v(t)=(2/3)t^{3/2}-(2/5)t^{5/2}+C. Since v(1)=4/15, C=0. Thus v(t)=(2/15)t^{3/2}(5-3t). For t>0, velocity is zero exactly at t=5/3 s.

after.name: Question 12
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=\sqrt{t}-{t}^{3/2}$, where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=\frac{4}{15}\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=1\,\text{s}$, determine the moment in time when the particle is stationary.
after.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (\sqrt{t}-{t}^{3/2})\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3/2}-\frac{2}{5}{t}^{5/2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1)=\frac{4}{15}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{15} & =\frac{2}{3}(1)^{3/2}-\frac{2}{5}(1)^{5/2}+C \\ \frac{4}{15} & =\frac{2}{3}-\frac{2}{5}+C \\ \frac{4}{15} & =\frac{4}{15}+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3/2}-\frac{2}{5}{t}^{5/2}.$

Now, we find the moments in time when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3/2}-\frac{2}{5}{t}^{5/2}=0 \\ \frac{2}{5}{t}^{3/2}(\frac{5}{3}-t) & =0 \\ t & =0,\,\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t>0$, the particle is stationary when $t=\frac{5}{3}\,\text{s}.$

23t3/2−25t5/2=025t3/2(53−t)=0t=0,53.

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, given by the function a(t)=t1/3−1, where t>0 is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity v=4m/s when t=8s, determine the moment in time when the particle is stationary.

a

b

c

d
t=6427s
e
t=934s
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating gives v(t)=(3/4)t^{4/3}-t+C. Using v(8)=4 gives C=0. For t>0, setting v(t)=t((3/4)t^{1/3}-1)=0 yields t^{1/3}=4/3, hence t=64/27 s.

after.name: Question 13
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)={t}^{1/3}-1,$ where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=4\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=8\,\text{s},$ determine the moment in time when the particle is stationary.
after.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ({t}^{1/3}-1)\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{t}^{4/3}-t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(8)=4.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =\frac{3}{4}(8)^{4/3}-8+C \\ 4 & =12-8+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{3}{4}{t}^{4/3}-t.$

Now, we find the moments in time when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4}{t}^{4/3}-t & =0 \\ t(\frac{3}{4}{t}^{1/3}-1) & =0 \\ t & =0,\frac{64}{27}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t>0,$ we discard the solution $t=0.$ Therefore, the particle is stationary when $t=\frac{64}{27}\,\text{s}.$

after.name: Question 15
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=3\sqrt{t}-1,$ where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=1\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=1\,\text{s},$ determine the moment in time when the particle is stationary.
after.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (3\sqrt{t}-1)\text{d}t \\  & =2{t}^{3/2}-t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(1)=1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =2(1)^{3/2}-1+C \\ 1 & =1+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=2{t}^{3/2}-t.$

Now, we find the moments in time when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2{t}^{3/2}-t & =0 \\ t(2\sqrt{t}-1) & =0 \\ t & =0,\,\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t>0,$ we discard the solution $t=0.$ Therefore, the particle is stationary when $t=\frac{1}{4}\,\text{s}.$
